summary: This article explains how the equator, the line of zero latitude, and the North and South Poles, Earth's two most extreme points, mark opposite ends of our planet's climate.
introduce: Read the title “The Equator and the Poles” aloud and ask each student to write one question they hope the article will answer. Collect a few questions, then explain that today they will find the one big idea that ties all the details together.

keyTerms.def: having a lot of moisture or wetness in the air
changing or happening with the seasons of the year
plants growing in a particular area

challengeTerms.def: one half of the Earth, divided by the equator or another great circle
the strength or amount of something, such as heat or light
the spreading out of something over a wider area

discussion: Do you agree or disagree that I would find it easier to live near the equator than near one of the poles? Use evidence from the article to explain.
Explain how the angle of sunlight affects the climate of the equator and the poles.
struggling: Pre-teach humid, seasonal, and vegetation with pictures or gestures, then let weak readers complete a main-idea-and-details web with a partner.
gifted: Ask strong readers to read a challenging version and write a short paragraph that uses hemisphere, intensity, and dispersion to state the main idea of the article in their own words.
